payload.root_cause: dragonfly-operator (deployed via bjw-s app-template) emits a NetworkPolicy on the Dragonfly CR that allows port 9999 (admin port) ingress only from pods labeled control-plane=controller-manager. The bjw-s app-template gives the operator pod app.kubernetes.io/* labels but NOT that kubebuilder label, so the operator cannot reach :9999 on the dragonfly pods to query dataset-load status and elect a master. Result: no pod gets role=master, the dragonfly Service has no endpoints, authelia cannot connect to redis at 10.43.135.100:6379 and crashloops.

payload.correction: FIRST PUT (data_rate_kbps=12000 + advertising_rates=true, but preference left at auto) was SILENTLY CLAMPED by the controller. GET-after-PUT (T1 attempt 1) showed advertising_rates took (false->true) but data_rate_kbps REVERTED to 1000 on all 4 SSIDs — classic UniFi silent-field-drop. Root cause: minrate_setting_preference=auto makes the controller recompute/ignore the manual data_rate_kbps. This is the exact footgun the verify-before-report rule guards against; rc=ok was a false positive.
payload.delta_to_record: 10.4.57 wlanconf min-rate model: to set a MANUAL 2.4GHz floor you MUST set minrate_setting_preference=manual; with it on auto the data_rate_kbps field is silently clamped to the computed default (1000). advertising_rates is honored independently of preference.

payload.lesson_applied: 2026-06-13 move-shutdown: setting nodown while client I/O was still active caused OSD PGs to block (512 slow ops, node01 drain hung). Fix that worked = scale CLIENTS down FIRST. This plan quiesces all client workloads BEFORE touching any Ceph flag, and only sets nodown once clients are quiesced.

rollback.abort_is_safe: Up to STEP 3 everything is reversible: flux resume, scale workloads back up, CNPG un-hibernate, ceph osd unset all flags. Cluster returns to current green state.
rollback.bringup_reverse: power network -> CP -> workers -> ceph GATE 2 (mons+osds up) -> unset flags (nodown,norecover,nobackfill,norebalance,noout) -> GATE 3 active+clean -> flux resume -> un-hibernate CNPG -> scale workloads back up -> Hestia re-enable 4 automations.
rollback.if_clients_wont_quiesce: Do NOT set nodown. Investigate stuck writer; if a StatefulSet won't drain, leave it and abort the shutdown rather than force flags with active I/O (that is exactly the 2026-06-13 failure mode).
rollback.if_pgs_block_after_flags: If slow ops / blocked PGs appear (the 512-slow-op signature), STOP - do not power nodes. Unset nodown, let I/O settle, escalate to Atlas.

sequence: STEP 0 (parallel, Hestia): HA safe-state - pause the 4 automations, record they were ON (rack-relocation Hestia A1).

STEP 1 SCALE CLIENTS DOWN FIRST (Heph): (a) flux suspend all app Kustomizations + HelmReleases so nothing re-reconciles workloads back up; (b) scale app Deployments/StatefulSets to 0 across media/home-automation/tools/etc; (c) CNPG hibernate postgres16 (clean primary shutdown, NOT delete); (d) scale Dragonfly, influxdb, pgadmin to 0. GOAL: zero client I/O to Ceph before any flag.
STEP 2 CONFIRM I/O QUIESCED (Heph): ceph status shows client io ~0 op/s; no rbd/cephfs writers left. Only THEN proceed.

STEP 3 CEPH QUIESCE FLAGS (Heph, runbook Heph §2): ceph osd set noout; norebalance; nobackfill; norecover; then nodown LAST and only because clients are now quiesced. Confirm flags listed in ceph status. NO ceph osd pause.

STEP 4 GRACEFUL NODE SHUTDOWN (OPERATOR, runbook Heph §3): talosctl shutdown WORKERS first (.81 .82 .83) then CP last (.84 .85 .86). Run from OPERATOR terminal - talosctl port 50000 is firewalled from this sandbox (verified: no route to host).
STEP 5 NETWORK LAST (Iris, runbook Iris §4): only after all 6 nodes + NAS confirmed off, power network edge-inward.

payload.plan: New small app kubernetes/main/apps/observability/monitoring-orphan-scan/ (own lifecycle/RBAC, does NOT touch the kube-prometheus-stack HelmRelease). unattributed_restart_finding.answer: The log CONFIRMS it was a deliberate restart request, but does NOT identify who made it.
unattributed_restart_finding.conclusion: Record as UNATTRIBUTED. Ruled out: no automation, script, scene or configuration.yaml entry calls homeassistant.restart (grep clean); no Kubernetes-side eviction/OOM (exit 100 = HA restart-requested, and the container was not killed); not Atlas (he made no write before 09:31:30); not me (my restart command at that moment was rejected by the permission system and did not execute). Plausible but UNPROVEN remaining origin: a human-initiated restart from the HA UI, mobile app or a kiosk session — note 09:25:11 shows kiosk-related service activity (switch.pixel_tablet_scherm), so a browser session was live in that window. I am not asserting that as the cause.
unattributed_restart_finding.evidence: Retrieved via kubectl logs --previous on the pre-restart container. 09:29:07.126 a full YAML configuration re-read begins (visible as annotatedyaml parsing /config/themes/... and re-registering bluetooth wrappers) — this is the config-validation pass homeassistant.restart performs — and the very next log line is 'Found 2 non-daemonic threads.', i.e. a graceful stop. That is the homeassistant.restart signature, not a crash: no traceback, no fatal error, no OOM, and the FP2 UndefinedError at 09:22:42 is 6.5 minutes earlier and non-fatal.
unattributed_restart_finding.question: Atlas asked whether anything in the log explains the 5th HA exit at 09:29:07 CEST, which neither he nor I initiated.
unattributed_restart_finding.recommendation_to_make_this_attributable: Either drop 'call_service' from the recorder exclude list (cost: recorder growth), or add a logger override for homeassistant.core at info/debug. Both are separate changes and I did not make either.
unattributed_restart_finding.why_the_caller_cannot_be_identified: 1) HA does not log the context/user of a homeassistant.restart at INFO level; 2) the recorder config in configuration.yaml explicitly excludes event_types: [call_service], so there is no recorded audit row for the service call; 3) logbook/history exclude the automation domain as well.

payload.the_underlying_fragility: A mobile_app notify SERVICE name is derived from the config-entry device_name, which the Android/iOS companion app can change WITHOUT any action in HA. When it does, HA silently deletes the old service and creates a new one. Nothing that referenced the old name errors until it next fires — and for a critical-alert path that can be weeks. This is exactly what happened on 2026-07-11. A rename is not a rare event; it happens on app reinstall, phone replacement, or the user editing the device name in the companion app.
payload.topic: Should these call sites use a notify GROUP instead of a hardcoded per-device service? (Atlas asked me to recommend, not restructure.)
payload.what_actually_closes_the_hole: Neither approach detects the failure. The real gap is that a broken critical-alert path was invisible for 12 days. Recommend ALSO a synthetic canary: a scheduled automation (weekly) that posts a self-test through the same webhook + notify path and raises a Prometheus/Loki-visible signal if the notify step errors — so the alerting path is itself monitored. Without that, any future rename is again only found by accident.

why_a_notify_group_helps_and_why_it_is_n.does_not_fix: A notify GROUP whose member service has been renamed still fails — the group forwards to a dead service. It reduces the blast radius from N automations to 1 config line; it does NOT make the failure self-healing or loud.
why_a_notify_group_helps_and_why_it_is_n.helps: A notify group (notify: - platform: group, name: critical_push, entities: [...]) gives a STABLE indirection point: automations reference notify.critical_push forever, and only ONE line in configuration.yaml has to be corrected after a rename. It also makes it trivial to fan out to a second device (Jurre's / Niko's phone, or the Galaxy Tab) so a single dead endpoint no longer means zero delivery.
why_a_notify_group_helps_and_why_it_is_n.important_nuance: Groups can reference notify ENTITIES rather than legacy services. notify.s25_ultra_sander is an ENTITY whose entity_id survived the 2026-07-11 rename unchanged (only its friendly name changed). Referencing the entity via action: notify.send_message with entity_id: notify.s25_ultra_sander would therefore have SURVIVED this exact failure mode, because entity_ids are stable across device renames while service names are not. That is arguably the stronger fix and I would pair it with the group.

followup_3_canary.failure_detection_design: The push cannot announce its own failure, so detection is push-independent. (a) IN-RUN: capture before_ts = states('notify.s25_ultra_sander'); push; wait 30s; compare after_ts. If timestamp did NOT advance -> the path is dead -> raise persistent_notification.create (in-HA card, visible on dashboards, no push needed) + logbook.log. If advanced -> dismiss any prior failure card. (b) CROSS-RUN watchdog automation notify_path_watchdog, daily 09:15: if now - as_datetime(states('notify.s25_ultra_sander')) > 8 days -> persistent_notification + logbook. This catches the case where the canary automation itself is disabled/broken/HA restarted into a bad state, and generalizes to ANY 8-day gap in delivery. Heartbeat uses the notify entity timestamp directly (Test A proved the legacy service advances it) so NO new input_datetime/input_text component is added (avoids a top-level-key add that could force a forbidden restart).
followup_3_canary.mechanism: New automation notify_path_canary. Weekly Monday 09:00 (+ manual via event notify_canary_run / automation.trigger). payload.problem: IOT-VLAN (6226f5bddd6f9706a46a66cb) is a member of the 'Internal' zone (67862226fe53ff1afe6e9de1) alongside CLIENT-VLAN and SERVER-VLAN, and Internal->Internal is 'ALLOW Allow All Traffic'. Firewall is 82/82 predefined, 0 user-created. Measured proof of the exposure: the Shelly at 172.16.4.20 gets HTTP 200 from Home Assistant at 172.16.2.237:8123.
risk_notes: Creating a zone triggers a firewall ruleset regeneration on the UDM. Brief; window is off-peak (Thu 10:30 CEST).

HA runs hostNetwork and reschedules across 172.16.2.81/82/83 — verified empirically that its source toward IOT is the node IP on the physical NIC ('ip route get 172.16.4.20' = via 172.16.2.1 dev enp89s0 src 172.16.2.81), NOT a pod CIDR address. Any source-scoped rule must therefore use CLIENT-VLAN 172.16.2.0/23, never a single node IP.
UniFi mDNS reflection is re-originated by the gateway; whether reflected packets are evaluated as IoT->Internal is UNKNOWN in advance. T6 measures it rather than assuming.
rollback: Primary: DELETE the new 'IoT' zone -> UniFi returns its network to the default Internal zone, restoring today's allow-all behaviour. Verify by re-running T2 and expecting code=200 again.
If the zone will not delete while policies reference it: disable/delete the user-created IoT policies first, then delete the zone.
Secondary: PUT the Internal zone re-adding 6226f5bddd6f9706a46a66cb to network_ids.
Full-revert fallback: also revert chg-2026-07-30-001 (Shelly back to VDHFEMFLEX via WiFi.SetConfig; sta1 fallback already armed), which removes the device from the affected segment entirely.
Escape hatch: the UDM GUI firewall page can disable any policy in one click if API writes misbehave.
steps: 1. POST /proxy/network/v2/api/site/default/firewall/zone {name:'IoT', network_ids:['6226f5bddd6f9706a46a66cb']}. Expect UniFi to move IOT-VLAN out of Internal implicitly (a network belongs to exactly one zone) and to auto-generate a predefined policy matrix for the new zone.
2. Read back BOTH the zone list AND the generated policies before touching anything else — do not assume the generated defaults.
3. Reconcile the generated matrix against intended_matrix; add/adjust only what differs. Pace writes >=1-2s apart (UniFi 10.x rate-limits with 429).
4. Re-verify with real traffic in both directions.
test_plan: T1 ZONE MEMBERSHIP: GET firewall/zone -> a zone named 'IoT' exists containing ONLY 6226f5bddd6f9706a46a66cb, AND 'Internal' no longer lists it. Both halves must hold; a network in no zone, or in two, is a fail.

T2 REAL TRAFFIC, IoT -> Internal MUST BREAK: Shelly HTTP.GET http://172.16.2.237:8123/ must go from code=200 (baseline) to a connection error. This is the whole point of the change; if it still returns 200 the change has FAILED regardless of what the config says.

T3 REAL TRAFFIC, IoT -> External MUST SURVIVE: Shelly HTTP.GET http://1.1.1.1/ must still return err '-4 response too big' (which means it connected). Plus Shelly.GetStatus cloud.connected must stay true and sys.time must keep advancing.

T4 END-TO-END, Internal -> IoT MUST SURVIVE (user-visible): from HA drive switch.verlichting_schuur on -> device Switch.GetStatus output=true with apower>0 -> off -> output=false. Same functional test as chg-001, re-run under the new policy. An HTTP 200 to /rpc alone is NOT sufficient.
T5 PUSH PATH MUST SURVIVE: flip the relay at the device; HA entity state must follow unprompted (proves the local_push websocket still holds across the zone boundary).

T6 mDNS: zeroconf browse from the HA pod must still see 172.16.4.20 on _shelly._tcp/_http._tcp. If it does not, record it honestly and decide whether to widen the 5353 rule or accept losing auto-heal (fixed reservations mean it is not load-bearing).

payload.important_nuance_for_future_readers: The final matrix contains BOTH 'ALLOW IoT->Internal (Return)' at idx=30000 AND 'BLOCK IoT->Internal' at idx=2147483647. That is not a contradiction and not a hole: the ALLOW is the stateful return companion auto-created by create_allow_respond on the Internal->IoT rule, so it only matches traffic belonging to connections INITIATED from Internal. New IoT-initiated connections hit the catch-all BLOCK — measured in T2, not assumed.
plan_deviations: PLANNED an extra 'IoT->Internal ALLOW udp/5353' rule to preserve HA's zeroconf auto-heal. NOT CREATED — T6 measured that mDNS reflection SURVIVES the IoT->Internal block on its own, because UniFi reflects via the gateway and the predefined 'IoT->Gateway Allow mDNS udp/5353' + 'Gateway->IoT Allow All' already cover it. Result is STRICTER than designed with no loss of function. This is why T6 was written as a measurement rather than an assumption.

payload.reason: User: the vloerverwarming automation was failing and left the pump off too long. Wants it fixed, with failure detection.
payload.summary: Replace the timer-driven pump automation with a self-healing time-triggered design + a watchdog that detects failure and verifies the pump actually draws power.

fix: Replaced the timer trigger with a plain daily TIME trigger at 11:00. A time trigger fires every day regardless of any prior state, so it cannot deadlock.
State is now held in input_datetime.vloerpomp_laatste_run (durable, survives restarts) instead of a timer's internal countdown.
The exercise only runs if the pump has not run in >24h, so real heat demand also counts as exercise and the pump is not cycled unnecessarily.

Added power verification: 45s after switching on, if sensor power is not >10W it sets input_boolean.vloerpomp_storing and pushes a notification. This catches a dead pump or an unplugged socket, not just a failed command.
New automation Vloerverwarmingspomp Watchdog: daily at 12:00, alerts if the last run was >48h ago OR if the beheer automation is not 'on'. That is exactly the failure the user hit.
Both use the CORRECT notify service notify.mobile_app_galaxy_s25_ultra (the stale mobile_app_s25_ultra_sander is what broke health-notify, inc-2026-08-27-001).
payload.open_question: The automation only reacts to sensor.woonkamer_verwarmen. sensor.slaapkamer_jurre_verwarmen and sensor.slaapkamer_niko_verwarmen also exist. If those rooms are also on floor heating the pump should run for them too - deliberately NOT changed, since altering heating logic without knowing the hydraulic layout could leave rooms cold.
payload.rollback: Restore /config/automations.yaml from /config/automations.yaml.bak-20260829-104925, then automation.reload.
payload.root_cause: The old automation's anti-seize cycle depended on timer.24hr_vloerpomp_timer, and the timer was ONLY restarted at the END of a cycle. If the automation was ever disabled, or HA restarted while the timer was idle, the timer never fired timer.finished again and the cycle stopped permanently and silently. Found the timer sitting 'idle' - the deadlock was live. Meanwhile the pump was stuck ON at 44W with zero heat demand, because with the automation off nothing turned it off.
payload.side_fix: Found and fixed the same {\} malformed-JSON default in ha-cli.sh cmd_call that I had already fixed in cmd_ws. It made every 'ha-cli.sh call' and 'ha-cli.sh reload' return HTTP 400. This masked the reload failures during this change - direct curl reloaded fine.

payload.design_decision_17C: SETBACK TO 18C (device min_temp), NOT hvac_mode off. Rationale: (1) 18 vs 17 is thermally inert for a 15-min vacancy, the compressor idles either way; (2) using 'off' recreates the exact bug class being fixed - on return Aanwezig would see 'off' and have to re-derive mode from temperature, and in the 18-22C dead band it would correctly leave the unit off, so on a mild day the user returns to a dead unit; preserving the mode means you return to the mode you were running; (3) off/on at 15-min granularity risks compressor short-cycling plus Tado restart delay; (4) keeps 'off' an unambiguous 'deliberately shut down' signal that both the 18:00 Kantoor Avond automation and the new window guard depend on. Cool setback = 26C (max_temp 30, valid).
findings_that_change_the_brief: BLOCKER: binary_sensor.kantoor_bezet is a STUB. Its configuration.yaml:459 template references binary_sensor.presence_sensor_fp2_<FP2_ID>_presence_sensor_1/_2 with the literal placeholder string FP2_ID. Only ONE FP2 exists in HA (f08e = kitchen); no office FP2 was ever paired. The template therefore always evaluates false. Confirmed: 1 sample in 168h, uniques = off. So 'Aanwezig has never fired' is NOT (only) caused by the != off condition - the trigger source can never go on. Dropping the condition is still correct and necessary but will NOT by itself make the pair live. Reported to Atlas, not fixed here: configuration.yaml is a different resource and picking a presence source is a design decision.

The Kantoor Z-Wave multisensor motion (binary_sensor.multisensor_motion_detection, same device d51c68cc as the illuminance) also has 1 sample in 168h - it never reports. Illuminance on the same node updates 218x/24h, so the node is alive; motion looks unconfigured (association/report interval). Not a drop-in presence replacement without Z-Wave work.

Setpoint inconsistency: the 08:30 one-shot sets heat 20 / cool 21, but the requested occupancy setpoints are 21/24. Aanwezig will immediately override the morning setpoint. Flagging, implementing as requested.

judgements.18C_decision: SOUND. 18 is the device floor, so it is the maximum setback achievable without hvac_mode off. judgements.race_in_last_triggered_guard: NOT RACY IN PRACTICE. HA sets last_triggered after conditions pass and before actions run, so the ordering semantics are correct. payload.note_on_ownership: Atlas has acknowledged the delay_on instruction as its own error. That resolves attribution, not the defect: the deployed configuration still does not deliver the approved outcome and must be corrected before this change can close.
remediation_advice: 1. REOPEN the change. Do not re-close until the user physical walk-in test is confirmed. Hestia own T4-FALLBACK already said this.

2. Set delay_on to 45 seconds (delay_on: {seconds: 45}); keep delay_off: 15 min UNCHANGED. Justified from the measured distribution, not convention: p50=31s and 26/48 episodes fall in the 29-40s band, which is the PIR own un-retriggered reset - anything below ~35s is indistinguishable from a single pass-through trip. The distribution has a hard cliff between >=30s (47/48) and >=40s (22/48), so 45s sits cleanly on the far side and selects only episodes where the PIR was RETRIGGERED, i.e. motion at two separate moments >=30s apart - the physical signature of stayed in the room rather than walked through. 45s admits 19/48 = ~6.3 latches/day versus 2.0/day at 120s (3x more sensitive) while still rejecting 60% of episodes. It also bounds worst-case latency: an occupant arriving at the desk latches within ~45s instead of never. 40s (22/48, ~7.3/day) is the acceptable more-sensitive variant; below 35s the discriminator collapses and every pass-through latches. This is the textbook PIR pattern - short on, long off - and delay_off 15min is what carries sitting-still, exactly as the file comment says.
3. Raise the hvac==off cool branch in 1747224001001 from > 22 to >= 23 to match the documented design intent and clear the current 22.67 reading.
4. Reconcile the setpoint conflict with 1734200001001: either align the morning cool setpoint to 24 or make Aanwezig not raise an already-active cool setpoint. As shipped they fight.
5. Extend the evening shutoff to weekends, OR have Afwezig set hvac_mode off when the room is below the cool threshold. Without this a Saturday latch runs the unit indefinitely.

6. Replace the now-false STUB paragraph in the descriptions of 1747224001001 and 1747224001002 with a dated chg-2026-08-30-005 note stating the pair is LIVE on binary_sensor.multisensor_motion_detection and what it will actuate.
7. Add 1734200001001 to the change record blast-radius list.
8. Item B and the rollback plan need no rework - both accepted as-is.

(b) condition: time with after/before is HA core and change-independent; an end-to-end test of it would be testing Home Assistant, not this change. design.B_boundary: A bare 'time after 12:00 before 23:00' condition is re-evaluated before the dim and before the off, so a run started at e.g. 22:55 stops at the boundary and hands over to B. B still catches the room via its at_2300 trigger and its all_clear_15m/light_on_quiet triggers. Restore-on-return is deliberately NOT time-gated (it repairs this automation's own dim; B cannot fire while presence is back).
design.all_clear: byte-identical to B's condition template (md5 of whitespace-normalised string = 90177756cc1e, verified equal to B's). Used verbatim in the template trigger, the condition block, and negated in both wait_templates. FP2 zone3 off AND FP300 woonkamer off AND tv_woonkamer_2 not in on/playing AND woonkamer/platenspeler/keuken/bar_2 each != playing.
design.latch_rearm_safety: input_boolean.turn_off on adaptief_bg_vanavond_gedaan is the LAST action and is only reachable after this automation's own light.turn_off. Two independent guards make a user's manual off unable to reach it: (1) the action sequence re-evaluates 'at least 1 of the 3 lamps is on' immediately before the dim AND immediately before the off - if the user switched them off, that bare condition aborts the run before the latch action; (2) nothing in this automation triggers on a light going OFF, so a manual off never starts a run that could reach the latch. Manual off therefore leaves the latch set and A does not re-light.
design.no_lux: Triggers are absence-only (template all_clear, sun window_start, light->on while quiet). No numeric_state on any illuminance entity anywhere. The lux-based auto-off removed by chg-2026-07-21-005 is NOT reintroduced. Lux is read only for the RESTORE brightness value, never as an off trigger.
design.restore: scene.create snapshot_entities of the 3 lamps taken immediately BEFORE dimming; on presence return scene.turn_on restores exact pre-dim brightness AND colour. Fallback when the transient scene is missing (e.g. HA restarted mid-run): light.turn_on with A's lux-scaled brightness template, byte-identical to A's Woonkamer branch. Never a hardcoded 100%.
design.scope: ONLY light.woonkamer, light.woonkamer_lamp, light.woonkamer_lamp_2. Kitchen (5) and bar (2) lamps are never referenced in any action. light.woonkamer_smartplug_woonkamer_raam (4th living-room light) deliberately NOT included - out of the brief's scope.

rulings.d1_deviation: ACCEPTED, and Themis was wrong. R1 as I specified it was based on a false premise about Home Assistant semantics: I asserted that a bare failing `condition:` inside an if/then halts the run. It does not - it aborts only the nested sequence and execution falls through to the following top-level actions. Hestia implemented my wording literally, reproduced the defect, captured trace e6b300a0 showing the fall-through reaching action/9, and fixed it with an explicit if -> stop. That is a more faithful implementation of my INTENT (do not restore, do not turn off, do not re-light, halt) than my literal wording was. The deviation is exactly what an engineer should do when a QA instruction is wrong: implement it, prove it insufficient with evidence, fix it, and record why. The rationale is durably captured inline in the action alias WITH the trace id, so the next person to read the block cannot re-introduce the bug. Endorsed without reservation.
rulings.d1_severity_note: Worth recording that my R1 would have SHIPPED A NEW DEFECT had she not traced it. On the presence-returned path, where nothing should ever be switched off, the fall-through dropped the run into the turn-off branch and was halted only incidentally because GUARD 3/3 happened to fail too. With a partial dim_targets subset that fall-through could have switched off a lamp the user had just switched on. Round 1 blocked a defect; round 2 caught a defect I introduced. rulings.q1_darkness_gate_action16: KEEP IT. This is scope PRESERVATION, not scope creep, and deleting it would be the actual unrequested behaviour change. Under the rejected D1 design the re-light was performed by A, and A gates on lux<40. Dropping the latch mechanism while omitting the darkness precondition would silently produce something A would never do: re-light a bright room. Themis verified action/16 uses A's EXACT lux source-selection (FP300 illuminance when fresh <3600s, else the FP2 light_level) and the same 40 threshold, so behavioural parity with A is preserved rather than invented. It additionally carries an L >= 0 fail-safe that mirrors A's own 'Lux geldig (fail-safe)' condition, so when both lux sources are invalid the automation does nothing instead of lighting a room on garbage input - the correct failure direction. It matches the user's own words, 'returning to a dark room re-lights it'. And Hestia flagged it explicitly and offered to delete it rather than smuggling it in, which is the behaviour the gate wants. Keep.
rulings.q2_generalised_lesson: For future gates, including my own: locks are ephemeral by design and ops/locks/ is not an audit log. `git status` on that directory reflects only the committed baseline versus now, and says nothing about transient locks. A 'D' on a committed lock file does NOT imply an unheld lock. Lock discipline cannot currently be evidenced after the fact from the filesystem at all. RECOMMENDATION (separate change, ops tooling, not a condition of this gate): have `ops lock acquire` and `ops lock release` append actor/resource/reason/timestamp to an append-only ops/locks.log so the gate can verify lock discipline instead of inferring it. Until that exists, Themis will not raise a lock finding on absence-of-file alone.
rulings.q2_lock_finding_RETRACTED: MY FINDING WAS WRONG. I refute it in full and it must be corrected with the user. Hestia followed the lock protocol. Three points. (1) ops lock acquire only writes a file and release deletes it - there is NO audit trail, so the absence of a lock file proves nothing about whether a lock was held and correctly released. My inference 'no lock file now => no lock was ever held' was a non sequitur, because a released lock is INDISTINGUISHABLE from one never taken, and releasing after the write is the CORRECT behaviour I would otherwise have demanded. (2) The evidence I already had refuted me and I failed to reason about it: in my very first round-1 tool call the ops/locks/ directory mtime read 'Sep 5 09:56' local = 07:56Z. Atlas released chg-005's lock at 07:36:43Z (09:36 local). A directory mtime only moves when an entry is created or removed, so a 09:36 deletion cannot produce a 09:56 mtime. It is explained precisely by Hestia acquiring at 09:44:44 local and releasing at ~09:56 local, the latter matching her validated event at 07:56:16Z. (3) Corroborated again this round: ops/locks/ mtime is now 2026-09-05T17:25:29+0200 = 15:25:29Z, consistent with R3's lock held from 15:05:27Z and released after the writes. The ' D ops/locks/ha.config.automations_yaml' in git status was solely Atlas deleting chg-005's COMMITTED lock file; a transient lock created and released between commits never appears in git status at all.

Required as the guard for `continue_on_error: true`: without it a failed Tado refresh would silently fall back to the old broken behaviour. 1800 s chosen because measured post-refresh cloud lag p99 = 23.3 min, so 30 min passes normal operation with headroom while catching a stalled feed. payload.ruling_on_the_synthetic_positive: ATLAS ASKED FOR MY VIEW, NOT AGREEMENT. My view: closing on a synthetic positive IS acceptable here, and demanding a real hot-weekday compressor start before closure would be WRONG. Five reasons. (1) It is unbounded on weather - the change would sit open for an unknown number of days polluting the digest as a stuck change, and a stuck record is not a watcher. (2) The synthetic positive cannot be upgraded even in principle: a POSTed fake sensor state would be WIPED by the automation own action[0] update_entity before any branch reads it. You cannot fake your way past this automation - that is a property of the design, not a testing shortfall. A live positive is impossible by construction. (3) The untested direction fails SAFE. The unproven failure mode is the compressor NOT starting - the exact direction this change deliberately biases toward, and strictly better than the pre-change behaviour that ran the unit for 8h22m. (4) The positive path is not novel code. It is the pre-existing start branch with ONE constant moved, and the equivalence above:23.49 == >=23.50 was proven on 283 real samples with ZERO samples in the divergence gap. There is no new logic on the positive side to discover. (5) Cost of being wrong is comfort-only, self-reporting within the hour, and reversible in seconds via a byte-exact rollback artefact I verified matches the true pre-image. THEREFORE I will not hold this change for weather.

control_law.curve: B(A) = 100 * (1 - A/600) ** 1.2, evaluated on AMBIENT lux A, not on measured lux. Smooth continuous power curve, no step ladder.
control_law.fit_vs_user_anchors: A=0 ->100.0 (target 100); 50 ->90.1 (90); 150 ->70.8 (70); 250 ->52.4 (50); 400 ->26.8 (25); 600 ->0 (off). Max absolute error 2.4 percentage points across the whole range.
control_law.floor_and_hysteresis: When on, brightness is floored at 10% (the raw curve returns absurd sub-1% values near 600 lux and Hue at 1% is indistinguishable from off). ON/OFF uses hysteresis to stop chattering at the boundary: turn OFF at A >= 600, turn back ON only at A < 550.
control_law.why_this_family: Single-parameter, exactly hits the two endpoints the user pinned (0 lux = 100%, 600 lux = off) by construction, and the exponent 1.2 was solved from the 50-lux anchor and then checked against the other three. Monotone decreasing, C1-smooth, and its slope is bounded - which is what makes the stability proof below possible.

oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.fix_1_control_on_ambient_not_measured: The automation never feeds measured lux into the curve. It estimates ambient as A = max(0, L - k*B_now), where L is measured lux, B_now is the lamp's CURRENT brightness in percent read from light.kantoor's brightness attribute (0 if off), and k is the lamp's lux contribution per brightness-percent. Because the lamp's own contribution is subtracted out, A is invariant to what the lamp is doing, so the setpoint does not move when the lamp moves. This converts a positive-feedback loop into an open-loop map from daylight to brightness.
oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.fix_2_deliberate_under_compensation_for_: k is set to 0.6 * kappa_measured, i.e. deliberately LOW. Stability analysis: with true contribution kappa and estimate k, dTarget/dB = -s*(kappa-k) where s is the curve slope. Under-compensation (k < kappa) leaves a small NEGATIVE feedback term -> damped convergence. Over-compensation (k > kappa) would give POSITIVE feedback -> runaway to 100%. Choosing k below the measurement makes the unstable direction unreachable even if the calibration drifts by 40%.
oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.fix_3_bounded_loop_gain: Max curve slope s_max = dB/dA at A=0 = 100*1.2/600 = 0.2 %/lux. Loop gain g = s_max*(kappa-k) = 0.2*0.4*kappa = 0.08*kappa. g < 1 requires kappa < 12.5 lux per brightness-percent, i.e. the lamp would have to add more than 1250 lux at the sensor at full brightness to destabilise. kappa will be MEASURED during execution and this inequality asserted before the automation is enabled; if it fails I stop and report instead of shipping an oscillator.
oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.fix_4_deadband: Even with g<1 a discrete loop can hunt by a point or two. The automation only re-commands the lamp when |B_target - B_now| >= 10 percentage points. Inside the deadband it does nothing, which terminates any residual limit cycle outright.
oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.fix_5_clamps: A is clamped to [0,600] before exponentiation, so the base of the power is never negative (which would raise a template error) and the target is never out of range.
oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.residual: Because k is under-compensated, the steady state sits slightly DIMMER than the ideal curve when the lamp is on. That is the deliberate price of guaranteed stability and is at most a few percent.
oscillation_prevention_THE_KEY_DESIGN_PO.the_hazard: Lamp on raises measured lux -> curve says dim -> measured lux falls -> curve says brighten -> limit cycle. This is the single most likely way the feature fails.

responsiveness_finding_REPORT_BEFORE_BUI.consequence_for_this_change: The automation is built so it is correct-but-slow today and simply gets faster if the parameter change lands later. No part of the design depends on a fast cadence. Mitigations: (a) it also triggers on presence, so walking into a dark office acts immediately on the last known lux; (b) a /10-min time_pattern safety net re-evaluates; (c) the self-induced lamp step IS reported fast (it exceeds 200 lux), so the compensated loop settles in minutes, not hours.

responsiveness_finding_REPORT_BEFORE_BUI.root_cause_read_from_device: zwave_js/get_config_parameters on device d51c68cc84d57a7924e665c9ab4ff991 (kantoor FGMS-001): param 40 'Illuminance Report Threshold' = 200 lux, param 42 'Illuminance Report Interval' = 3600 s. The median 3617 s gap is exactly param 42. So the sensor only sends an unsolicited lux report when the reading moves by >= 200 lux, plus a forced heartbeat every hour.
responsiveness_finding_REPORT_BEFORE_BUI.why_this_matters_more_than_atlas_thought: The user's entire control band is 0-600 lux. A 200-lux report threshold means that inside that band essentially NO event-driven reports are generated - only the hourly heartbeat. Worse, the ONE thing that reliably does exceed 200 lux is the lamp switching on or off. So a naive lux-triggered automation would be driven almost entirely by its OWN actions and barely at all by daylight. That is the exact recipe for the oscillation failure mode.

payload.RULING_focus_mode_1004: ACCEPTABLE AS-IS, not a blocker, and NOT a regression - previously 1004 slammed the lamp to 100% with nothing to pull it back; now adaptive recovers it. But note an interaction nobody recorded: 1004 conditions on light.kantoor == on, which was almost never true before this change and is now true for much of the working day, so this change materially INCREASES 1004 firing probability. Worst case is bounded - at night the adaptive target is 100% anyway so there is no visible conflict, and in daylight recovery is fast because lux reports are frequent. Carry-forward, not a fail.
payload.RULING_manual_override: It is the behaviour the user specified (continuous tracking), so not a defect on its own. But it compounds the hunting: the user will naturally try to correct a hunting lamp by hand and will be overridden within seconds during daylight. Pull the override forward and bundle it with the damping fix.
payload.RULING_sequencing: Deviation is real and is NOT waived - but re-cutting the artefact is pointless: a re-cut produces a byte-identical file, buying nothing and costing a disruption in the user office. The remediation below subsumes it, and that fix MUST follow install-disabled -> QA -> enable. IMPORTANT AND UNCOMFORTABLE: had QA seen this pre-execution I would very likely NOT have caught the hunting either, because the evidence required a bright variable-daylight day that had not yet occurred. So the sequencing breach is NOT what caused the escape, and treating install-disabled as the fix would be learning the wrong lesson.

WHAT_IS_CORRECT_AND_VERIFIED.kappa_stability_reasoning: SOUND - re-derived independently by change-qa. B_next = f(A_true + (kappa-k)B); |f_prime| max = 100*1.2/600 = 0.2 %/lux at A=0; contraction needs 0.2|kappa-k| < 1 i.e. |kappa-k| < 5. With k=0.6 and kappa in [0.73, 2.0], |kappa-k| <= 1.4, gain <= 0.28. Also checked the endpoint she did not: fully STALE lux behaves as kappa=0, giving |0-0.6|=0.6 and gain 0.12 - still a contraction. Margin to instability is kappa >= 5.6, about 3x outside the independently-derived upper bound. Her planned-event wording that over-compensation gives runaway to 100% is overstated (positive feedback with gain<1 still converges), but the SHIPPED criterion in calibration-summary.md is the correct two-sided one and is conservative. The self-feedback loop does not oscillate.
WHAT_IS_CORRECT_AND_VERIFIED.reconciles_atlas_23_vs_27: BOTH ARE RIGHT, different questions. 27% was correct AT COMMAND TIME because br_now was 70 -> ambient 400.0 -> curve 26.76 -> 27. Atlas 23% is the NEXT target using the current br_now of 27 -> ambient 425.8 -> 22.7 -> 23; |23-27| = 4 < 10 so the deadband correctly holds and no re-command is issued. Deadband behaving as designed.

payload.WHAT_THE_BRIEF_SHOULD_HAVE_SAID: (1) Default order is install-DISABLED -> QA -> enable. (2) Where an end-to-end test genuinely requires the automation to be live, the brief must AUTHORISE a time-boxed supervised enablement up front, naming who watches it and for how long, instead of demanding a test that is impossible under the stated order. (3) NEW RULE the real lesson: for any control loop driven by an environmental sensor, the test plan must enumerate the OPERATING REGIMES (night / overcast / bright variable daylight) and the change may not CLOSE until evidence covers them, or until a stated soak window has elapsed. A single-window sample must not be generalised into a stability claim. Hestia surfacing the decision rather than hiding it was correct behaviour and should be affirmed.

checks_failed.name: production_stability_of_the_control_loop
checks_failed.reason: The lamp visibly hunts in daylight. Replaying the SHIPPED branch logic against the REAL 2026-09-09 sensor stream: in 4.9 h of occupied daylight (07:59-12:55Z) the automation issues 17 light service calls - 9 full on/off transitions plus 8 brightness re-commands spanning 10%..73%. Adjacent commands include 31%->73% in 94 s, 19%->56%->18% inside 10 min, and 27%->62% in 6.3 min. The lamp switches fully on/off roughly every 20 minutes while the user is at the desk. REPLAY IS VALIDATED AGAINST GROUND TRUTH, not asserted: it reproduces all 9 observed on/off transitions in the HA logbook to within 1.3 s, and both brightness values recoverable from live automation traces (12:43:26 -> brightness_pct 27, 12:49:42 -> brightness_pct 62).

checks_failed.name: false_premise_in_planned_and_validated_events
checks_failed.reason: The record states param 40 = 200 lux and param 42 = 3600 s mean there are essentially NO event-driven reports inside the 0-600 control band, only an hourly heartbeat, and cites 20 samples with median gap 3617 s over 24 h. That census was taken over a night + overcast window and does not generalise. change-qa measured 184 lux reports between 00:00Z and 12:55Z on 2026-09-09, many 2-3 s apart (e.g. 11:34:49, 11:34:51, 11:34:58, 11:35:00, 11:35:03). Param 40 is a DELTA threshold; real daylight swings 400<->2839 lux and breaches it continuously. The night-only regime (17:46Z-04:52Z, all 0.0, exactly hourly) is what the census actually sampled.

checks_failed.name: stability_claim_certified_against_an_unrepresentative_regime
checks_failed.reason: T7 OSCILLATION PROOF is genuine but tests only the SELF-FEEDBACK mechanism (lamp -> sensor -> lamp) during a single quiet late-afternoon sample. The mechanism that actually bites is INPUT NOISE: the control law is memoryless with no temporal filtering, and the 50-lux hysteresis band plus 10-point deadband were sized against smooth simulated ambient. Real ambient carries +/-1000 lux excursions within seconds, which swamps both. The record certifies a stability property that does not hold in the operating regime the user experiences.

checks_failed.name: transition_tail_corrupts_br_now
checks_failed.reason: Second-order contributor. br_now reads state_attr(light.kantoor, brightness) while a 5 s transition: may still be in flight. With lux reports arriving 2-3 s apart in daylight this reads mid-transition values, corrupting the ambient estimate. mode: single drops overlapping RUNS but does not cover the post-run transition tail.

remediation_advice: 1. HIGHEST VALUE - damp the input. Drive the control law from a FILTERED lux value (statistics sensor mean or filter platform time_simple_moving_average over ~5-10 min) rather than the raw sensor. This alone removes most of the hunting.
2. Widen the on/off hysteresis well beyond the noise floor (e.g. off >= 900, on < 450) and/or require the crossing to persist via a for: so a single passing cloud cannot toggle the lamp.
3. Add a minimum re-command interval (e.g. no more than one brightness change per 5 min). Cheap, directly caps visible churn, independent of 1 and 2.

4. DO NOT execute the recommended Fibaro param 40 -> 50 lux / param 42 -> 600 s change until 1-3 are in. REVERSED from the recommendation in the planned event: more frequent reports would make the hunting significantly WORSE, not better. This carry-forward must be corrected before anyone actions it.
5. Fix br_now during the transition tail - capture the commanded value in a variable or suppress runs within 5 s of the previous command.
6. Lighting hold: add for: 00:10:00 to the bezet_uit trigger INSIDE 1012 only, giving lighting ~25 min while climate keeps 15. Do NOT change the shared template sensor.
7. Add the input_boolean.kantoor_licht_override escape hatch and condition 1012 on it; rewire 1004 to set it.

T5 CADENCE AFTER (necessary, not sufficient): re-run the identical gap script over the post-change window and compare in-band statistics against T2. PASS requires event-driven in-band reports at gaps well under 600 s, plus a heartbeat floor at ~600 s instead of ~3600 s. Necessary but NOT sufficient - it proves the sensor talks more, not that the lamp does the right thing.

T6 END-TO-END USER-VISIBLE OUTCOME (the real test, and the point of the change): demonstrate that a GENUINE AMBIENT change inside the 0-600 band produces a lux report AND a corresponding brightness correction, with the lamp's own output NOT being the trigger. Evidence: (a) a joint timeseries of sensor.multisensor_illuminance and light.kantoor brightness; (b) the automation trace showing it fired on trigger id 'lux' (not 'tick', not 'bezet_aan') and issued light.turn_on with a NEW brightness_pct; (c) an ORDERING PROOF that the lux moved BEFORE the lamp did, so the report cannot have been self-induced; (d) the lamp's own read-back brightness attribute from the REST state API, not the value I sent. Today is variable and overcast, so real cloud transitions are available.

T7 STABILITY AT THE HIGHER REPORT RATE (the failure mode I flagged myself): at 50 lux the lamp's OWN swing will now definitely generate reports, which it mostly did not at 200 lux. Verify (a) the compensation A = clamp(measured_lux - 0.6*brightness_pct, 0, 600) still holds; (b) the 10-point deadband still suppresses self-induced correction - identify lux reports that arrive within seconds AFTER a lamp command and show the next automation evaluation took no action; (c) no monotone walk of commanded brightness across >=3 consecutive evaluations; (d) count light.kantoor brightness changes per hour before vs after - a large jump means hunting. If the loop destabilises that is a FINDING and I recommend the partial rollback of param 40, not a shipped hunting lamp.

T8 KAPPA SECOND DATA POINT: chg-2026-09-08-003 could only bound kappa to 0.73-2.0 because a full 0-100% lamp swing did not breach the 200-lux threshold and the hourly heartbeat blurred it into a falling ambient. At a 50-lux threshold a lamp step should be reported within seconds, which isolates it. Prefer an OPPORTUNISTIC measurement from a brightness change the automation makes by itself; only force a step if that does not occur. Compute kappa = delta_lux / delta_brightness_pct over a short window where daylight is quiet, compare against the 0.73-2.0 band and against the shipped k=0.6, and re-assert the stability inequality |kappa - k| < 5.

T9 BATTERY ACCOUNTING: record battery pre (100%) and post, and record the measured post-change reports/day so the drain is quantifiable in weeks rather than guessed. Battery percentage will NOT move measurably inside this change window - I will say so plainly rather than imply the cost was measured.

ROOT_CAUSE_RESTATED_FROM_MEASUREMENT.actual_cause: INPUT NOISE crossing an unguarded gate. The shipped 10-point deadband guards ONLY the brightness re-command branch. The on/off decision was guarded solely by a 50-lux hysteresis band (off at ambient>=600, on at <550).
ROOT_CAUSE_RESTATED_FROM_MEASUREMENT.not_self_feedback: My original stability proof was correct and is not the problem. Themis re-derived it independently; loop gain <= 0.28, contraction holds across the whole kappa band.
ROOT_CAUSE_RESTATED_FROM_MEASUREMENT.the_number_that_settles_it: median consecutive |delta lux| on the real 2026-09-09 stream is 440 lux, p90 is 801 lux, max 1504 lux. Peak-to-peak inside any 60 s window: median 950 lux. The noise is ~9x the entire hysteresis band. Flapping was inevitable.

THE_FINDING_THAT_CHANGED_THE_DESIGN.answer: SEVEN. True ambient genuinely swung 75 -> 1618 lux and legitimately crossed the 600-lux boundary 7 times. The shipped logic made 9. So the excess attributable to hunting is only 2 transitions, NOT 9.
THE_FINDING_THAT_CHANGED_THE_DESIGN.the_actual_fix: Stop switching the lamp off in response to daylight at all. While the office is occupied the lamp stays on and rides the curve down to a 10% floor. The 7 genuine daylight transitions then become invisible brightness changes instead of jarring full on/off events. This preserves tracking accuracy AND removes the user-visible defect, which no amount of filtering could do simultaneously.
THE_FINDING_THAT_CHANGED_THE_DESIGN.what_I_did: I built an IDEAL-controller benchmark: reconstructed true ambient (lamp contribution removed via kappa) and asked how many on/off transitions a perfect, zero-noise controller would make on 2026-09-09 during occupancy.
THE_FINDING_THAT_CHANGED_THE_DESIGN.why_this_matters: It means damping the input CANNOT be the main fix. I measured that directly: every filter/gate combination that meaningfully cut transitions also degraded the controller - a 30-min window got calls down to 1 but left the user in a genuinely dim office, unlit, for 65 minutes. Optimising for 'fewest service calls' converges on a lamp that does nothing. I nearly shipped that.

entity_choice.why: CMDB records these devices as local_push with Ws.enable=false, so HA holds an OUTBOUND websocket to the Shelly on TCP/80. The unifi tracker only measures AP association, so it is false-negative when a device is associated but unroutable, and false-positive for all ten at once whenever the unifi integration hiccups (documented instability: memory unifi-v10-poller-breakage, 429 rate limits). design.1_near_instant_turn_on: ACCEPT Atlas's proposal. Add trigger id 'pir' on binary_sensor.multisensor_motion_detection to 'on'. delay_on on kantoor_bezet is NOT touched - the climate pair keeps its calibrated 45 s.
design.2_turn_on_hoisted_above_interlock: Move the turn-on branch ABOVE the 300 s interlock, exactly as branches 'afwezigheid' and 'veiligheidsklep' already sit above it. The automation's own description already states the principle: 'Een veiligheidsvoorziening mag nooit onderdrukt kunnen worden door een snelheidsbegrenzer.' Restoring light to an occupied dim room is that class of action. No new flap risk: the only fast off-paths are the absence branch (needs bezet off >=10 min AND raw PIR off AND ownership) and the fel valve (needs 15 min sustained >1500 lux), so an unrestricted turn-on cannot ping-pong against either.
design.3_absence_branches_get_a_raw_PIR_GUARD: The absence branches now additionally require binary_sensor.multisensor_motion_detection to be 'off'. Physical justification: if the raw PIR is asserting right now, a person IS in the room, whatever the debounced template says. This is what actually kills the 20:40 incident. NO new stuck-on failure mode: kantoor_bezet is derived from the same PIR, so a stuck-on PIR already pins bezet 'on' and already blocks the absence branch today.
design.4_manual_override_via_ownership_inversio: Mirror the screen's auto_dicht inversion. New input_boolean.kantoor_lamp_door_automatisering. ON = this automation turned the lamp on and may turn it off. OFF = the lamp is off, or somebody else turned it on -> hands off. The controller sets the boolean ON immediately BEFORE its own light.turn_on (order matters: set-then-command, so no window where its own action looks external). A separate tiny automation clears the boolean when the lamp settles off.
design.5_ownership_gates_the_OFF_decision_ONLY: Deliberate scope limit. Brightness adaptation continues even on a human-turned-on lamp, because adaptive dimming is the feature the user asked for and gating it would mean one manual flip disables adaptation for the whole day. The fel safety valve also keeps working regardless of ownership - it needs 15 minutes of sustained >1500 lux so it cannot plausibly fire seconds after a human action, which was the actual complaint.
design.6_hue_group_artefact_defence: The ownership-clearing automation triggers on light.kantoor to 'off' FOR 10 SECONDS. The description documents a Hue group artefact where the group re-reports itself 'on' mid-fade (08:32:40.711 off -> 08:32:41.723 on -> 08:32:55.678 off) and the transition is 5 s. A 10 s hold means only a settled off clears ownership, so no transition artefact can strand the boolean.
design.7_walk_through_bounded: NEW trigger 'pir_uit' on the raw PIR to 'off' for 3 minutes, so the absence branch gets an evaluation opportunity that does not wait for the /10 tick.

payload.FINDING_cadence_correction: The brief states the sensor reports every ~15 min. Measured: the modal inter-sample gap is 299 s and 1546 of ~1768 gaps are 298-300 s. THE CADENCE IS 5 MINUTES. The rare multi-hour gaps are deep night, when light_level is pinned at 0 so the state object stops changing and the recorder writes nothing - not a dropout. Consequence: the responsiveness floor is 5 min, not 15, and a stale reading can cost at most one 5-minute step during the dusk transition.
payload.FINDING_worse_than_reported: The brief says the automation arms ~30 min after sunset. Over 10 evenings it is worse than that: on 4 of 10 it did not arm until 22:14, 22:45, 23:01 and 23:46. On those evenings the path light was effectively DEAD for the entire evening, not merely late. Cause: light_level lingers at small non-zero values (231, 3242) for hours and only reaches 0 late. Proposed threshold arms at 19:31-20:36 on all 10 evenings, i.e. within about 10 minutes of sunset.

sun_elevation_argued_both_ways.case_against_and_CHOSEN: Elevation is a PROXY; illuminance is the thing we actually care about. Gating on elevation would refuse light during a black thunderstorm at 15:00 - exactly when a path light is most useful. The two failure costs are wildly asymmetric: failing to light a dark path is a safety issue and is the users actual complaint, whereas lighting the path for 5 minutes on a gloomy afternoon costs a few watt-hours and nobody notices an outdoor lamp in daylight.
sun_elevation_argued_both_ways.case_for: A sun-elevation condition is immune to a dirty, obstructed or failed lux sensor, and it is perfectly seasonal - it would hold up in December where a 10-day September sample cannot speak.
sun_elevation_argued_both_ways.decision: Keep a PURE LUX THRESHOLD. No sun condition. Elevation was used as the DIAGNOSTIC to size the threshold - which is its proper role here - but not as a runtime gate.
sun_elevation_argued_both_ways.residual_risk_stated: The 10-day sample is early September. A dull December noon in NL, with the sun barely above 14 deg, could plausibly read below 48.9 lux on this shaded sensor and light the path. Consequence is trivial and arguably desirable. Recommend a review after the first winter month rather than pre-emptive complication.

threshold_derivation_NOT_a_round_number.mapping: Hue light_level is already a log10 scale: lux = 10**((light_level-1)/10000). So 55 = 1.01 lux = near total darkness, as the brief says.
threshold_derivation_NOT_a_round_number.step1_daylight_floor: Over 1769 samples / 10 days, the lowest light_level EVER recorded with the sun above 10 deg is 17866 (61.2 lux). Next lowest 19369 (86 lux). That is the hard empirical ceiling - go above it and we start lighting the path on dull afternoons.
threshold_derivation_NOT_a_round_number.step2_arming_requirement: The light_level at the evening crossing, per day, ranges 14703..16666 with the highest at 15913 on 2026-09-05. To catch dusk on the FIRST available sample we must sit above ~15913.
threshold_derivation_NOT_a_round_number.step3_midpoint: The separating band is therefore [15913, 17866]. Because light_level is ALREADY log-scaled, the arithmetic midpoint is the geometric mean in lux. T = (15913+17866)/2 = 16889.5 -> T = 16890 = 48.9 lux. It is derived from the two empirical edges, not chosen for roundness.
threshold_derivation_NOT_a_round_number.step4_validation: At T=16890: 0 of 1351 samples with sun above 10 deg would fire. 5 of 1511 with sun above 4 deg would fire, all at elevation <= 5.6 deg - genuinely gloomy low-sun moments where lighting the path is correct, not a false positive. Margin to the darkest daylight reading ever: 1.25x in lux.

PROOF OF PORT-53 HIJACK: dig @198.51.100.77 chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl A  (198.51.100.77 = RFC5737 TEST-NET-2, unroutable, nothing can answer there) -> 'flags: qr aa rd ra' / 'chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl. 5 IN A 172.16.2.200'. An authoritative (aa) TTL-5 answer from an address that does not exist = the UDM answered.
Same forgery from dig @185.253.5.0 (CLIENT-VLAN DHCP secondary): 'flags: qr aa rd ra' / 'chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl. 5 IN A 172.16.2.200'

Hijack is SELECTIVE, which is why it was not noticed: dig @1.1.1.1 example.com -> 'flags: qr rd ra' (NO aa) TTL 127, real upstream answer; dig @8.8.8.8 zzz-nonexistent-probe-argus.vdh-ict.nl -> NXDOMAIN, no aa. The UDM forges ONLY for names in its static-dns table and proxies everything else.
findings.impact: Two consequences. (1) The consistency argument in the review brief ('Sander's business domain already discloses internal addressing, so the pattern is established') is not true. The estate DOES currently hold the no-private-IP-in-public-DNS line, and this change does not break it either. The justification was wrong; the outcome happens to be fine. (2) Any agent on this LAN that verifies a public DNS fact with dig/nslookup against a resolver IP is measuring the UDM, not the internet. This already injected one false statement into a change record today.
findings.remediation: Record a memory: on this LAN, public-DNS assertions MUST be made over DoH (https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query or https://dns.google/resolve) or from an off-LAN vantage point. dig @<resolver-ip> is only ever evidence about the UDM. Recommend this becomes a standing rule for Iris, Athena and Argus.
findings.title: FALSE PREMISE: cloudnas.vdh-ict.nl does NOT publish an RFC1918 address in public DNS. All 'dig @public-resolver' verification performed from this LAN is unsound.

evidence: Parent is signed: dig +short @1.1.1.1 vdh-ict.nl DS -> '39809 8 2 A4D850839179F51DF71024395CDABBFD42C753399258C34C9C8389BEF8274039' (alg 8 RSASHA256, digest 2 SHA-256)
Raw DoH wire query with DO bit for chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl A -> rcode=3 (NXDOMAIN), AD=1, answers=0, authority=8, response 1041 bytes. Same for api.lan.vdh-ict.nl: rcode=3, AD=1, authority=8.

Authority section carries a real NSEC3 denial chain: SOA vdh-ict.nl + RRSIG(SOA) keytag 50686 alg 8, plus NSEC3 records e.g. 'kgo4spmq3lb3dnhkasfe29f2f2m1f30a.vdh-ict.nl 50 = 1 0 1 AB KO9R004NM6I75H23EBS36TCHT91HAFEM SRV RRSIG' each with its own RRSIG. NSEC3 flags field = 0, i.e. OPT-OUT IS NOT SET, so the non-existence proof is complete and not skippable.

The UDM's forged answer carries no signature: dig @172.16.2.1 chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl A +dnssec -> 'flags: qr aa rd ra', 'EDNS: flags: do', answer 'chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl. 5 IN A 172.16.2.200', ZERO RRSIG records returned. The DO bit is echoed but nothing is signed.
lan.vdh-ict.nl has no delegation today: dig @1.1.1.1 lan.vdh-ict.nl NS -> no NS, only 'vdh-ict.nl. 1800 IN SOA ns1.openprovider.nl. dns.openprovider.eu. 2025012601 ...'
findings.impact: The port-53 hijack (SEC-01) rescues plain-DNS clients on any VLAN, but it CANNOT rescue DoH (443) or DoT (853) - those bypass the redirect entirely, and I demonstrated they return NXDOMAIN. The stated audience is 'family on the home LAN' on phones and laptops. Firefox, Chrome Secure DNS, iOS/macOS encrypted-DNS profiles and any downstream validating resolver will get an NXDOMAIN that is cryptographically PROVEN, not merely absent. A strict validator that is handed the UDM's unsigned A record while holding that proof should treat it as bogus. This is an availability and support-burden finding, and it is the durable one Themis asked about: it outlives the change and is not fixed by anything in the change.
findings.impact_on_this_change: None retroactively - nothing listens on 443 yet, so no family member can observe the breakage today. It becomes real the moment myPKA P2 lands a listener.
findings.remediation: Choose one before P2, do not discover it from a family bug report: (a) accept split horizon and document that encrypted DNS must be off on family devices - brittle, fails silently, I do not recommend it; (b) delegate lan.vdh-ict.nl to deSEC and publish the RFC1918 A records there for real - DNSSEC-clean and works everywhere including DoH, but it publicly discloses internal addressing, which is the line SEC-01 shows the estate is currently holding; (c) delegate lan.vdh-ict.nl INSECURELY (NS at openprovider, no DS) so the subtree is unsigned - removes the authenticated-denial sharp edge, still NXDOMAIN for DoH clients; (d) put the user-facing name under a zone that is not a signed public parent (the estate already runs vdh.lan - verified dig @172.16.2.1 nas.vdh.lan -> 172.16.2.246) and keep lan.vdh-ict.nl solely for the ACME TXT side. (d) is the cleanest security posture but costs a rename that myPKA is already building against.
findings.title: Split horizon under a DNSSEC-signed parent: the public zone returns an AUTHENTICATED denial of existence for both new names. DoH/DoT and validating clients will not see the platform.

evidence: Intent per the review brief: delegate lan.vdh-ict.nl to deSEC for ACME DNS-01 TXT records.
Today there is no delegation and therefore no such path: dig @1.1.1.1 lan.vdh-ict.nl NS returns no NS, only the vdh-ict.nl SOA.

Verified the ACME challenge name is NOT shadowed by the new rows, so the delegation is technically compatible: dig @172.16.2.1 _acme-challenge.chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl TXT -> 'status: NXDOMAIN', 'flags: qr rd ra' (no aa) = forwarded upstream, not answered locally.
findings.impact: Once lan.vdh-ict.nl is a real delegated zone, whoever holds the deSEC token can publish A records under it AND obtain valid Let's Encrypt certificates for chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl. LAN clients are protected because the UDM's local row wins, but a family member off-LAN (mobile data, or on-LAN with DoH enabled per SEC-02) would reach an attacker-controlled host presenting a browser-trusted certificate for the exact name they were taught to type. That is a credible phishing chain against the household AI platform.
findings.remediation: When the delegation is made: scope the deSEC token to TXT records only if deSEC supports per-rrtype restriction, store it in 1Password via ExternalSecrets rather than on the Studio, and publish a CAA record so certificate issuance for the zone is constrained. Revisit severity at delegation time; it is low today only because the zone does not exist.
findings.title: Future deSEC delegation creates an off-LAN impersonation path for the family AI platform if the deSEC API token is compromised.

resolver_behaviour_characterised.consequence_bad: No record of ANY type can ever be seen by a LAN client at the exact names chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl and api.lan.vdh-ict.nl other than the A row. CAA is the one that could bite: if a CAA record is later placed at the exact host name it will read as NODATA from inside the LAN. Public issuance is unaffected because Let's Encrypt validates from the internet.
resolver_behaviour_characterised.consequence_good: ACME DNS-01 via deSEC is compatible with these rows. The challenge label _acme-challenge.<host>.lan.vdh-ict.nl is a SUBdomain and is forwarded upstream, so cert-manager's in-cluster propagation self-check will see the deSEC TXT rather than a locally forged NODATA.
resolver_behaviour_characterised.port_53_is_universally_redirected: Queries to ANY destination IP on udp/53 are answered by the UDM for names in its static-dns table. Demonstrated against 198.51.100.77 (RFC5737 unroutable) and 185.253.5.0. Not defeated for tcp/443 DoH or tcp/853 DoT.
shadowing_is_EXACT_NAME_ONLY_but_covers_: dig @172.16.2.1 chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl TXT -> 'status: NOERROR', 'flags: qr aa', ANSWER: 0, authority = locally synthesised 'vdh-ict.nl. 1800 IN SOA ns1.openprovider.nl. ...' = NODATA, answered locally, NOT forwarded
dig @172.16.2.1 chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl MX -> 'status: NOERROR', 'flags: qr aa', ANSWER: 0 = same NODATA behaviour
dig @172.16.2.1 chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl AAAA -> empty (matches Iris test T11)
dig @172.16.2.1 _acme-challenge.chat.lan.vdh-ict.nl TXT -> 'status: NXDOMAIN', flags WITHOUT aa = forwarded upstream
dig @172.16.2.1 nothere.lan.vdh-ict.nl A -> 'status: NXDOMAIN', flags WITHOUT aa = forwarded upstream

payload.DEVIATION_1_app_start_sensor_does_not_ex: Atlas wrote: the app start time is available as a Fully sensor once Change A lands; find the right entity. It is NOT. I read site-packages/homeassistant/components/fully_kiosk/sensor.py directly: the integration ships exactly 9 sensors - batteryLevel, batteryTemperature, currentPage, screenOrientation, foregroundApp, internalStorageFreeSpace, internalStorageTotalSpace, ramFreeMemory, ramTotalMemory. lastAppStart is returned by the Fully deviceInfo API but never surfaced as an entity, and no template can reach coordinator data. Getting it requires a rest: sensor polling the Fully API, which needs the Fully admin password in secrets.yaml. That is credential handling, i.e. auth-adjacent, so per Atlas own instruction it needs an Argus security_review FIRST. I therefore split it out as chg-2026-09-16-004 and did NOT execute it. This automation references sensor.keuken_tablet_app_start and DEGRADES GRACEFULLY while it does not exist: R1 still restarts but logs honestly NIET te verifieren instead of claiming success, and R4 computes age -1 and stays silent. When chg-004 lands both rules activate with no further edit to this automation.
payload.DEVIATION_2_cap_window: Sander said per 24 h. I implemented a FIXED 03:55-03:55 window, not a true rolling 24 h. A true rolling window needs a 3-slot input_datetime ring buffer; I judged the extra fragility not worth it for a safety net. Needs Sander confirmation. Documented in the automation description itself so the next reader is not misled.
payload.DEVIATION_3_start_url_hardcoded: The R5 template trigger compares against the literal https://keuken.bluejungle.net/dashboard-keuken/keuken because trigger templates cannot see action-scope variables. findings.evidence: Transport is plain HTTP with the credential in the URL query string (Fully offers no header auth on this API). fully_kiosk/const.py:12 already polls the same host:port with the same password every 30s, so the credential is on the wire ~2,880x/day today; scan_interval: 30 (patch L23) makes it ~5,760x/day. CLIENT-VLAN 172.16.2.0/23 is the household client VLAN and carries Wi-Fi clients, so an attacker with L2 position (guest device, compromised phone) can ARP-spoof and capture it. Password is 8 chars alnum (verified len=8, isalnum=True).
findings.remediation: Set scan_interval: 60. That halves the ADDED exposures (2,880 -> 1,440/day) and breaks neither requirement: R1 waits 5 minutes (5 polls at 60s) and R4 is evaluated by a /30-minute time_pattern. Separately, consider lengthening the Fully Remote Admin password at the next tablet touch - 8 alnum chars on an unrate-limited LAN HTTP endpoint is thin.
findings.title: scan_interval 30 doubles how often an 8-char admin password crosses CLIENT-VLAN in cleartext

findings.evidence: Checked Hestia's rejected MQTT alternative directly. (a) The tablet is not publishing: `mosquitto_sub -t 'fully/#' -W 12` on the live broker returned 'Timed out' with zero messages, against a passing control (`$SYS/broker/version` -> 'mosquitto version 2.0.22'). (b) fully_kiosk's manifest `"mqtt": ["fully/deviceInfo/+"]` is a DISCOVERY declaration only - `grep -rn 'mqtt|deviceInfo' fully_kiosk/coordinator.py` -> exit 1, zero hits - so even if the tablet published, the integration would not turn it into a lastAppStart entity; a hand-written mqtt: sensor would still be required. (c) Security-wise the MQTT path is NOT an improvement: it removes a password from secrets.yaml but requires storing broker credentials ON the consumer Android tablet, which is a lower-trust store than a root-only Ceph RBD PVC. Conclusion: the rest: sensor is the correct design, not merely the only one.
findings.remediation: None. Recorded so the option is not re-litigated.
findings.title: No credential-free alternative exists in scope; the MQTT option would move the secret somewhere WORSE

findings.evidence: Patch L36-37: `{{ (value_json.lastAppStart | as_datetime).isoformat() }}`. The availability template (L34-35) only checks `is defined and truthy`, not parseability. If Fully ever returns a differently-formatted lastAppStart, as_datetime returns None and .isoformat() raises a template error. Not a security issue - the resulting log record contains the template and entity_id, not the credential - but it produces a hard error rather than a clean 'unavailable'.

payload.design: Single long-running watcher (mode: single) built as repeat(count 40) + wait_for_trigger. At the TOP of each iteration it captures eta_ref from the live payload; because an iteration only advances past the wait after a push has been sent, eta_ref IS the last NOTIFIED ETA, not the previous poll. The >=15 min test (>=900 s) is evaluated inside the wait trigger against eta_ref, so poll jitter of a few minutes never pushes. This needs ZERO new helper entities and leaves no persistent state to clean up.

sizing_justification.limitrange: defaultRequest cpu 50m / memory 128Mi; default (limit) memory 1Gi; PVC min 1Gi max 100Gi. No cpu default limit and no container max/min for cpu - a LimitRange max on a resource forces a limit onto every container, which is the throttling footgun above. default memory limit is 1Gi rather than 512Mi because the VolSync restic mover indexes a 50Gi repo and 512Mi is a plausible OOM.
sizing_justification.measured_headroom: 3 workers, 7950m allocatable CPU and ~60GiB allocatable RAM each. Current requests 49%/49%/66% CPU and 51%/22%/31% memory. Ceph: 3.00TB raw, 230GB used, 2.77TB raw free; ceph-blockpool replica=3, so ~920GiB usable free.
sizing_justification.quota: requests.cpu 4, requests.memory 8Gi, limits.memory 16Gi, pods 20, persistentvolumeclaims 20, requests.storage 400Gi, services.loadbalancers 1, services.nodeports 0
sizing_justification.why_NO_limits_cpu: DELIBERATE. Quoting limits.cpu would force a CPU limit on every container via the LimitRange, and CFS throttling is exactly wrong for a git server (clone bursts, git gc, CI). Memory is the resource that actually causes node-level harm, so limits.memory is quota'd and limits.cpu is not.
sizing_justification.why_loadbalancers_1: Direct guard for P4. The Cilium l2-pool is 172.16.2.0/23 which spans 172.16.2.0-172.16.3.255 and overlaps the CLIENT-VLAN DHCP range. This caps devtools at exactly ONE LoadBalancer IP - Iris's :22 service - so nothing in this namespace can silently claim a second LAN address.
sizing_justification.why_nodeports_0: devtools must never expose a NodePort; everything goes through the gateway or the single approved LB.
sizing_justification.why_requests_cpu_4: Programme footprint at full build (P1-P7) is forgejo 100m + forge-pg 2x200m + volsync mover ~50m + a P7 Actions runner ~2000m = ~2.6 cores. 4 leaves headroom without a follow-up quota edit blocking P7. 4 cores is ~17% of worker CPU.
sizing_justification.why_storage_400Gi: Peak concurrent claim is larger than the steady state because VolSync clones the source PVC: forgejo-data 50Gi + volsync snapshot clone 50Gi + volsync cache 5Gi + forge-pg 2x20Gi = 165Gi, plus headroom for a CNPG instance rejoin and future growth. 400Gi is ~43% of usable Ceph free, so it is a real cap, not a rubber stamp.

BACKUP_OFFSITE_FINDING.consequence_if_ignored: Putting forge-pg under cnpg-backups would ship Forgejo's database - issues, PRs, review comments, user emails, SSH public keys, repo names and topology for CLIENT repositories - to Azure nightly, in gzip, NOT encrypted. That is squarely inside what chg-2026-09-15-003 lists as NOT covered ('off-site copying of client repos ... default remains NO').
BACKUP_OFFSITE_FINDING.evidence: kubernetes/main/apps/storage/minio-offsite-mirror/app/cronjob.yaml runs 'for bucket in cnpg-backups volsync' and rclone sync's each to Azure Blob nightly at 04:30. Any CNPG cluster that writes to s3://cnpg-backups/* is therefore copied OFF-SITE to Azure.
BACKUP_OFFSITE_FINDING.mitigation_authored: destinationPath: s3://forge-backups/forge-pg. 'forge-backups' is NOT in the rclone loop, so the mirror never sees it. A comment in cluster.yaml states this explicitly so the next person does not 'tidy' it into cnpg-backups.
BACKUP_OFFSITE_FINDING.residual_gap_1_encryption: Atlas asked whether gzip-not-encrypted is acceptable for a code forge. It is NOT ideal and I am not silently matching the pattern. CNPG barman only offers SERVER-side encryption (encryption: AES256 = S3 SSE-S3). Our MinIO has no KMS configured (no MINIO_KMS_* env in the minio HelmRelease), so SSE-S3 would fail. There is no client-side encryption option in barman. So: forge-pg backups sit gzip-only on the Synology NFS volume. Recommendation: accept for now because the data never leaves the house, and raise a SEPARATE change to add MinIO KES/KMS - which would also close the identical gap that postgres16 (Authelia + Home Assistant + Grafana) has TODAY.
BACKUP_OFFSITE_FINDING.residual_gap_2_no_offsite: The direct consequence of honouring 'no off-site for client repos' is that the forge has NO off-site backup at all. A house fire destroys Ceph, the Synology and the forge together. Sander should confirm he accepts that, or approve an encrypted-only off-site path as a separate decision. I am not making that call.
BACKUP_OFFSITE_FINDING.verdict: BLOCKER-CLASS FINDING, resolved in the design. Do not use the default bucket.

payload.judgement_separate_vs_shared: SEPARATE cluster, recommended. Reasoning recorded in the report to Atlas. Short version: postgres16 holds Authelia, Home Assistant, Grafana and lldap - the household's auth and history. Forgejo will hold client data and will be reachable by CI runners (P7). Sharing would put a client-data schema and a CI-reachable credential inside the same instance as the family's auth store, and would make every Forgejo schema migration a household-critical maintenance window. Cost of separate is 2 extra pods (~400m CPU request, 2Gi RAM) on a cluster at 49-66% CPU request.

deliberate_omissions_CONFIRMED.mechanism: If a ResourceQuota specifies limits.cpu, the API server requires every pod in the namespace to declare a CPU limit or admission fails. To keep operator-created pods (CNPG instance pods, VolSync restic movers, Helm test hooks) admissible you would then need a LimitRange default cpu, which stamps a CFS quota onto every container. So quoting limits.cpu really does force CPU limits estate-wide in that namespace - the causal chain Heph describes is real, not hand-waving.
deliberate_omissions_CONFIRMED.non_blocking_caveat: With no container max on memory, a single pod could declare limits.memory 16Gi and absorb the whole namespace limit budget. Acceptable in a single-tenant namespace; worth remembering if P7 ever puts an untrusted CI runner in here.
deliberate_omissions_CONFIRMED.verdict: Heph reasoning is CORRECT. Confirmed, not merely accepted.
deliberate_omissions_CONFIRMED.why_that_is_right_here: CPU is compressible; CFS throttling on a git server adds latency to exactly the bursty operations that matter (clone, git gc, CI jobs) while protecting the node from nothing. Memory is incompressible and is what actually causes node-level harm, which is why limits.memory IS quoted at 16Gi and defaulted to 1Gi. The asymmetry is deliberate and textbook-correct. No challenge.

heph_unproven_claim_b_RULING.BETTER_PROCEDURE_THAN_THE_ONE_RECORDED: Heph recorded just test ci, which he could not run (no docker). That is unnecessary. Once the namespace exists on main, kubectl --dry-run=server exercises the FULL admission chain - LimitRange mutating admission and ResourceQuota validating admission - and persists nothing. Exact commands: (1) kubectl -n devtools get resourcequota devtools -o jsonpath={.status.hard} - must echo all 8 keys, a rejected key never appears in status; (2) kubectl -n devtools run q1 --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9 --restart=Never --dry-run=server -o jsonpath={.spec.containers[0].resources} - must show requests cpu 50m / memory 128Mi and limits memory 1Gi; (3) kubectl -n devtools run q2 --image=registry.k8s.io/pause:3.9 --restart=Never --overrides for 5 CPU --dry-run=server - must be REJECTED with exceeded quota: devtools. heph_unproven_claim_b_RULING.reason_1_confined_blast_radius: If the claim is wrong the failure mode is: pods in devtools are rejected at admission. devtools is empty at land and stays empty until P2. heph_unproven_claim_b_RULING.reason_2_semantics_are_deterministic: Every dimension the quota constrains has a matching LimitRange default: quota requests.cpu <- defaultRequest cpu 50m; quota requests.memory <- defaultRequest memory 128Mi; quota limits.memory <- default memory 1Gi. There is no unmatched dimension. defaultRequest memory 128Mi <= default limit 1Gi, so the LimitRange is internally consistent. No cpu default limit and no cpu max means no CPU limit is required, and the quota does not constrain limits.cpu - consistent. This is specified K8s behaviour, not a guess.

sizing_verified_against_live_cluster.STARVATION_ANSWER: NO. Atlas asked whether landing this quota could starve anything existing. It cannot. A ResourceQuota reserves nothing - it is a namespace-scoped admission cap that can only ever REJECT creations inside devtools. It cannot evict, cannot reserve capacity, cannot influence scheduling in any other namespace. A LimitRange is likewise namespace-scoped. The only cluster-wide hazard anywhere in this change is the kustomization.yaml build failure above, and that is a reconciliation hazard, not a capacity one.

checks_failed.substantive_finding_for_argus: This is not a formality. secrets.yaml maps the MinIO ROOT credentials into devtools. barman therefore gets root-equivalent access to the ENTIRE MinIO instance, not just forge-backups: cnpg-backups (the household's authelia/home_assistant/grafana/lldap dumps), volsync, mac-mini-backups, thanos. checks_failed.reason: The planned/executed payload states: 'CNPG PVCs are NOT pruned by Flux (owned by the operator) - they must be deleted deliberately, which is the desired safety property.' That is false, and it inverts the actual behaviour. Verified empirically against the live estate: postgres16's PVCs carry ownerReferences [{kind: Cluster, name: postgres16, controller: true}]. Flux install.yaml sets prune:true, so reverting the commit deletes the Cluster; Kubernetes garbage collection then deletes the Cluster-owned PVCs; and sc/rook-ceph-block has persistentVolumeReclaimPolicy=Delete (confirmed on the live PV behind postgres16-1), so the RBD images and all data are destroyed. The pvc-protection finalizer only delays this while pods still mount. The CNPG-generated -app Secret is Cluster-owned too and goes the same way. A revert does NOT leave the volumes behind for deliberate cleanup - it DESTROYS them. Only the barman bucket survives, which is the one part of the statement that is right.
